rows.title: Color
rows.text: If you are a swellshark or a Scyliorhinus retifer catshark, your eye has a single visual pigment, and in the Australian swellshark no cone opsin was detected at all. A review lists a cone pigment in the dusky, blue, tiger, gummy and Port Jackson sharks, and two rays, Glaucostegus typus and Aptychotrema rostrata, have three kinds of cone. Nobody has measured how many kinds of color-sensing cell most sharks have, so what color looks like to you is unknown.

cites.taxon: Carcharhinus obscurus, Prionace glauca, Galeocerdo cuvier, Mustelus antarcticus, Heterodontus portusjacksoni

rows.note: Replaced "reports" with "lists". Left out the Greenland shark (R1) and all wavelength numbers, since none compare or picture anything here.

rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: A human reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart, and the sharks measured in these records see less fine detail than that. If you are a great white shark, the retinas of two young ones give a best case of about 5 cycles a degree, and a review lists 11 for the bigeye thresher and 2 for the brown-banded bamboo shark. For most other sharks and rays, nobody has measured how sharply you see.
rows.note: Replaced "reports" with "lists" for the voice check. Left out Port Jackson, wobbegong, epaulette, skate and stingray figures to keep the row short; the row stays at i because most species are unmeasured.

rows.title: Sharpest band
rows.text: If you are a Port Jackson shark or a lemon shark, a horizontal streak across your retina holds more densely packed cells, so you see most sharply along a horizontal band. If you are a great white, you have a patch of sharpest vision instead, and it looks at the zone above and to the sides of your head. In most other sharks and rays nobody has mapped the retina, so nobody knows which of these you have.
rows.note: Left out R5 (small-spotted catshark): its quote names the species but does not state the value. Left out R1 because it is a skate.

rows.title: Pace
rows.text: A lamp flashing 60 times a second looks steady to a human, and the sharks measured so far stop seeing flicker at lower rates than that. If you are a brownbanded bamboo shark, the limit is about 45 flashes a second, if you are a blacknose shark it is about 15, and if you are a small-spotted catshark it is about 3. Nobody has measured it in most sharks and rays, so for them the number is unknown.
rows.note: Left out the ranges in rays (R17 reaches 60 Hz) to keep the sentence true; said "sharks measured" only.

rows.title: Two eyes
rows.text: The patch of space ahead where both your eyes see at once varies a lot from one species to the next. It is about 10 degrees wide in a lemon shark, 11 in a blacknose shark, 13 in a bonnethead, 35 in a scalloped hammerhead and 50 in a winghead shark, and in rays it is about 45 in a cow-nosed ray and 70 in an Atlantic stingray. Nobody has measured it in most other sharks and rays, so if you are not one of these, nobody knows how much your two eyes overlap.

cites.taxon: Dasyatis sabina, Rhinoptera bonasus, Raja eglanteria, Urobatis jamaicensis

rows.note: No human overlap figure in the records, so no human comparison. Eye placement left out for lack of a record.

rows.title: Electric sense
rows.text: A flatfish buried in sand gives off a faint electric field, and if you are a small-spotted catshark, you find it by that field alone and give the same feeding response to two buried electrodes. If you are a scalloped hammerhead, a juvenile turns toward a prey-like electric field from about 30 centimeters away. Electric sense has been measured in only a few sharks, rays and rabbit fish, and for most others, including you if you are none of these, nobody has measured it.
rows.note: Left out pore counts (R4-R6) and cell firing (R1) to stay within three sentences; "centimeters" used for the 30 cm figure.
